title: Japanese Nutmeg-yew: Ancient Nutmeg-yew Trees You Can Visit
meta_description: A slow evergreen conifer. Three of Japan's three great kaya trees are mapped here, plus one whose nuts a lord ate before a war-deciding 1615 campaign.
intro: Torreya nucifera, called kaya in Japan, is a slow evergreen conifer that looks the same in February as in August, which is part of why its oldest specimens went unnoticed for centuries. Three of the four mapped here are named, without much argument, as Japan's three great kaya: one in Maebashi at 8.1 metres round, one in Saitama traditionally dated to the 1030s, one on private farmland near Hamamatsu that visitors view from the road. The fourth, at Nagoya Castle, carries a stranger claim to fame: the first Owari lord ate its nuts before marching on Osaka in 1615, in the campaign that finished the Toyotomi and secured Tokugawa rule for two and a half centuries, and his successors kept eating them every New Year after. None of the four gives up its age easily; growth rings, girth surveys and shrine tradition all disagree, sometimes by centuries.
